title: Mala Copa in Brownsville brings upscale to the outdoors - NewsBreak
text:
By Travis M. Whitehead ,
6 hours ago
B ROWNSVILLE — The waitress in her perfect black uniform steps into the outdoor dining area and approaches a table where four young people enjoy the early evening.
“Everything good out here?” she asks.
They say it is all very good and I know it must be true. I see a long plate of something that must have been very good because I can’t tell what it was even though I’m sitting close by.
I have never been in a place like Mala Copa, where the greater dining area is outside and feels more like an upscale lounge area. The shifting of colors soft and smooth and rhythmic has a calming effect, further accented by the fading sun and the breeze over Pablo Kisel Boulevard.
Two menu items immediately grab my attention: oyster Rockefeller as an appetizer and mariscada al mojo de ajo.
Every time I see “oyster Rockefeller” I remember driving to Saltillo, Mexico about 25 years ago and knowing nothing of Mexico or Saltillo or driving in Mexico. I dove in blind to this trip to Saltillo — there were two actually — with little knowledge or planning.
So I really didn’t know what to look for when I arrived in Saltillo, but I did find myself in a restaurant where I was surprised to find “oyster Rockefeller” on the menu. I did not know they served such things in Mexico. I really was going in blind.
That introduction to “oyster Rockefeller” stayed with me so clearly that I instantly remembered the encounter when I took a seat at Mala Copa at 3101 Pablo Kisel Blvd.
Mariscada al mojo de ajo took me to a plastic table on the sand beneath a thatched roof where I had mojarra al mojo de ajo. I was on the beach of Playa Azul in the Mexican state of Michoacan and it was also many years ago. I remember this not so much for the dinner but for the novelty of sitting at a table right on the bare sand and watching the surf with the white foam and the blue sky and the seabirds.
I liked also the simplicity of that experience. The meal was a simple grilled “mojarra” — sand perch, on a plate and it was very good.
However, there is nothing simple this evening about mariscada al mojo de ajo at Mala Copa in Brownsville. The menu describes this item as having shrimp, octopus, fish and calamar “smothered in our chef’s garlic sauce.”
The memories of these two dishes compel me to order both, and while I wait I take in more fully the sights and the sounds of Mala Copa.
Heavy Spanish rap fills the air and the woven bamboo pendent lamps extend from the ceiling and spread their soft lighting, and beyond the wooden wall paneling the lights of the businesses along Pablo Kisel brighten as the darkness grows stronger.
The waitress, the lovely waitress with the perfect skin and the perfect smile fresh and beautiful, brings drinks and a sparkler to the table next to me. The young man with the black cap and the white shirt is celebrating his birthday and I think it is a birthday I can no longer remember.
This is an upscale place and it is a fancy place, but it is not an exclusive place. It is rather a place for anyone to treat themselves to a taste of the luxurious. Two young men in faded jeans and T-shirts take a seat nearby. Two women, one in a leopard print top, sit at a stool overlooking Pablo Kisel and the waitress serves them drinks.
My appetizer arrives, and it looks very much like the oyster Rockefeller I enjoyed 25 years ago in Saltillo and it is very good. A very few minutes later a huge plate of shrimp and fish and calamar arrives, with small octopi twisting their tentacles across everything.
This mojo de ajo is definitely not Playa Azul, but something quite different and extraordinary and memorable, and I am glad I will carry part of it home with me in a box.
